passage:
In the kasba school at the foot of the hills, Ayesha's Hindi essay came back with a red mark on one word and a note: "Very good." She read only the red mark. That night under the bulb she copied the whole essay again, twice, until her wrist ached and her eyes burned. When she was done she tore up both attempts.
Keerthana Ma'am found her before assembly, hollow-eyed. "The essay was very good, Ayesha. Why the rewriting?"
"One word was wrong."
"One word. Next time fix that word and move on. Try to be a little better than last month, not flawless." She handed the essay back. "Pick one small thing to improve this week."
Ayesha chose spelling, and slowly put the essay in her bag.

qa.q: What did Ayesha's Hindi essay get on one word?
qa.a: It got a red mark on one word.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha copy the essay out again and again?
qa.a: She could not accept anything short of perfect: she read only the red mark and ignored the 'Very good'.

qa.q: What small step did Keerthana Ma'am suggest?
qa.a: She suggested picking one small thing to improve this week and aiming to be a little better than last month, not flawless.

qa.q: How does Keerthana Ma'am see the essay and Ayesha's rewriting?
qa.a: She sees the essay as very good and the rewriting as unnecessary, and the hollow eyes tell her that Ayesha is punishing herself.

grounding: A girl in a small town punishes herself for one small error; a teacher suggests aiming for improvement and one small step, not perfection.

passage:
Sunday. Got 94 in the physics test. Everyone in class was happy for me. I came home and redid the whole paper at my desk till two in the morning because of the six marks I lost, and cancelled football with Imran as punishment. That's what I do. Anything less than full marks and I sort of sentence myself. Imran knocked this morning and asked why I'd skipped football. I said I didn't deserve it. He sat on my bed and said, 'Bhai, you're doing to yourself what nobody else would dare to do to you.' That stuck. So today I tried something new. Instead of 'perfect', I wrote 'one percent better' on a sticky note. I looked at the six marks, found it was one formula I'd mixed up, practised that for twenty minutes, and stopped. Then I went to football. Felt weird. Felt good. Tomorrow, one more small thing.
- Farhan

qa.q: What did Farhan write on the sticky note?
How did Farhan feel about scoring 94?
qa.a: He felt it wasn't good enough and was frustrated and harsh with himself over the six lost marks.

qa.q: What small step helped Farhan break the pattern?
qa.a: Fixing just the one formula for twenty minutes, then stopping and going to football.

qa.q: How does Imran see the way Farhan treats himself?
qa.a: As harsher than anyone else would dare to be, which worries him enough to speak up.

grounding: A diary of a teen who punishes himself for anything below full marks, trying small good-enough steps toward improvement instead.

passage:
Swati: did you submit the coding project?
Uday: no. deleted it
Swati: WHAT. it was due tonight
Uday: the animation lagged for half a second. it looked amateur
Swati: uday it was amazing. I saw it yesterday
Uday: half a second, swati. anyone would notice
Uday: I do this every time. if it's not perfect I trash it and then I hate myself for missing the deadline
Swati: ok. what if the goal isn't perfect, just better than last time?
Uday: better than last time is... anything. I didn't submit last time either 😅
Swati: exactly!! so submit yesterday's version, it's still in your drive right
Uday: yeah
Swati: fix the lag next week as version 2. small steps
Uday: ...ok. uploading
Uday: done. 11:52 pm
Swati: 🎉 proud of you
Uday: honestly feels lighter than deleting it

qa.q: Why did Uday delete the coding project?
qa.a: The animation lagged for half a second and it looked amateur to Uday.

qa.q: How does Uday feel after trashing unfinished work?
qa.a: Uday feels frustrated and self-hating for missing the deadline again.

qa.q: What did Swati suggest instead of perfection?
qa.a: Submitting yesterday's version and fixing the lag later as version 2, aiming for better, not perfect 👍

qa.q: How does Swati see Uday's project?
qa.a: Swati thinks it was amazing and that half a second of lag hardly matters.

grounding: A chat showing a teen who trashes work that isn't perfect, choosing a good-enough submission and small improvements instead.
